tip: English wastes 'water' with no article, but French needs the partitive: gaspille de l'eau = wastes some water. Uncountable things always take du, de la or de l'.
You don't trust someone directly in French – you 'make trust TO' them: faire confiance à. So it's lui, not le: Je lui fais confiance.
When two pronouns stack, me/te/nous come before le/la/les: te le, not le te. Je te le promets = I promise it to you, the reverse of English word order.
In a negative command the pronoun stays BEFORE the verb: Ne lui dis rien. Only positive commands push it after, as in dis-lui.
réfléchir à quelque chose = think about it. The à-phrase collapses to y, sitting before the verb: il y réfléchit = he's thinking about it.
en avoir marre = to be fed up. The en is baked into the idiom and can't be dropped: Nous en avons marre = we've had enough.
manquer flips the subject: Il me manque = I miss him, literally 'he is lacking to me'. The person missed is the subject; the one missing them is me/te/lui.
devoir means both 'must' and 'owe'. Here it's owe, and you owe TO someone: Nous lui devons beaucoup = we owe him a lot. So lui, not le.
In a positive command the pronoun hooks onto the verb with a hyphen: parle-leur = talk to them. parler à quelqu'un takes leur, not les.
répondre à quelqu'un = answer someone. French answers TO a person, so the pronoun is lui, not le: Tu lui as répondu?
Short adverbs like déjà slip between the two parts of the past tense: avons déjà réservé, not 'avons réservé déjà'. English keeps 'already' outside.
dépendre uses de where English uses 'on': Je dépends de mes parents = I depend ON my parents. The preposition rarely matches English.
After a preposition French switches to stressed pronouns: avec moi, not 'avec je'. Same with toi, lui, eux: Je la prends avec moi.
à emporter = to take away, to go. It's the standard phrase for takeaway food: le prenons à emporter = we're getting it to go.
A reflexive verb in a positive command swaps te for toi and attaches it: habille-toi = get dressed. Only positive commands make this switch.
trouver here means 'find' in the sense of opinion: Tu la trouves comment? = What do you think of her/it? Literally 'how do you find her?'
depuis + the present tense = have been doing: Nous y pensons depuis longtemps = we've been thinking about it for a long time. French stays in the present.
For body parts French uses 'the' plus an indirect pronoun, not a possessive: lui a coupé les cheveux = cut HIS hair, literally 'cut him the hair'.
apprendre stacks two à's: à a person, à an action. Il leur a appris à nager = he taught them to swim (leur = à them, à nager = to swim).
en stands in for 'any/some' of a thing: Tu ne m'en as pas donné = you didn't give me any. English can drop 'any', but French keeps en.
demander à quelqu'un = ask someone. French asks TO a person, so the pronoun is lui, not le: Nous lui avons demandé son avis.
son/sa agree with the thing owned, not the owner: son sac = her (or his) bag, because sac is masculine. The owner's gender is invisible.
parler de something = talk about it, and de + thing collapses to en: Ils en parlent = they talk about it. en sits before the verb.
French says 'less loud' for 'more quietly': parle moins fort = speak more softly. fort is the go-to word for volume, not 'loudly'.
attendre already means 'wait FOR' – no preposition follows: Tu les attends = you're waiting for them. Never add 'pour'.
retrouver = meet up with someone by arrangement (literally re-find them), not meet for the first time: Tu le retrouves après le travail?
Weather uses faire (to make), not être: il fait chaud = it's hot, literally 'it makes hot'. Same for il fait froid, il fait beau.
After quand, French uses the future where English uses the present: quand vous aurez fini = when you're done, literally 'will have finished'. Both actions stay future.
en + the -ant form = 'while/on doing': en rentrant = on your way home, while heading back. French compresses 'while returning' into en + verb.
To say why you're going somewhere, French just adds a bare infinitive – no 'pour': j'irai au marché acheter des fruits = go to the market to buy fruit.
dès + a noun = 'as soon as': dès notre arrivée = the moment we arrive. Where English needs a whole clause, French uses dès + noun.
